p.src: This poem subtly accords with the wondrous Way attained by the Great Sage Sun. Having secured the demon’s genuine treasure and tucked it into his sleeve, he rejoiced, saying, “That wretched demon took such pains to capture me, but truly it was no more than grasping at the moon in the water; if Old Sun wished to seize you, it would be as easy as playing with ice over a fire.” Concealing the gourd, he quietly slipped outside, resumed his true form, and shouted sternly, “Open the gates, fiends!” A lesser demon nearby said, “Who are you to come shouting here?” Pilgrim said, “Hurry and report to that old scoundrel of yours that I am Pilgrim Sun, come in person.”

p.src: The lesser demon hurried inside and reported, “Great King, someone called Pilgrim Sun has come to the gate.” The old demon cried in alarm, “Brother, this is terrible! We have stirred up the whole hornet’s nest. Pilgrim Sun is tied up with the Gold-Brocade Rope, and Reverse-Pilgrim Sun is inside the gourd; so how can there now be yet another Pilgrim Sun? His several brothers must all have come.” The second demon said, “Set your mind at ease, elder brother. This gourd of mine can hold a thousand men. I have put only one Reverse-Pilgrim Sun into it, so why should I fear any Pilgrim Sun? Let me go out and see him, and I shall put him in as well.” The old demon said, “Be careful, brother.”

p.src: The demon said, “Come over here. I shall not fight you, but if I call your name, will you dare answer?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “If you call me, I shall answer; but if I call you, will you answer?” The demon said, “When I call you, I have a precious gourd that can draw people inside; but what do you possess with which to call me?” Pilgrim said, “I too have a gourd.” The demon said, “If you have one, take it out and show me.” Pilgrim drew the gourd from his sleeve and said, “Look, you wretched fiend.” He gave it a shake and hid it in his sleeve again, for fear the demon might try to snatch it.

p.src: At the sight of it, the demon was greatly startled and thought, “Where did his gourd come from? How can it be exactly like mine? Even if they grew on the same vine, they should differ in size and be straight or crooked; so how can they be identical in every way?” He composed himself and called out, “Pilgrim Sun, where did that gourd of yours come from?” Pilgrim truly did not know its origin, so he took his cue and answered with a question: “Where did your gourd come from?” The demon failed to see through this ploy and took it for an honest question, so he recounted the whole origin from the beginning: “When chaos first divided and Heaven and Earth opened, the Supreme Patriarch assumed the name of Nüwa, smelted stones to mend the sky, and brought universal salvation to the world of Jambudvīpa. When he had mended the breach in the Qian sector, he saw at the foot of Mount Kunlun a strand of immortal vine bearing this purple-gold red gourd, which Lord Lao has preserved until the present day.” Hearing this, the Great Sage adopted the demon’s own account and said, “My gourd came from that very place as well.” The demon chief said, “How can you prove that?” The Great Sage said, “When clear and turbid first divided, the sky was incomplete in the northwest and the earth in the southeast. The Supreme Patriarch of the Way transformed himself into Nüwa and mended the breach in the heavens. On reaching the foot of Mount Kunlun, he found an immortal vine bearing two gourds. I obtained the male one, while yours is the female.” The monster said, “Never mind male or female. If it can hold people, it is a fine treasure.” The Great Sage said, “You are right about that. I shall let you try yours first.”

p.src: The monster was delighted. He sprang into the air, held up the gourd, and called, “Pilgrim Sun!” On hearing him, the Great Sage answered eight or nine times in a single breath, yet the gourd could not draw him in. The demon dropped back down, stamped his feet, beat his chest, and cried, “Heavens! I thought the ways of the world never changed, but even a treasure like this fears its husband: when the female sees the male, she no longer dares draw anyone in.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Put yours away. Now it is Old Sun’s turn to call you.” He swiftly turned a somersault and leapt aloft, holding the gourd with its base toward heaven and its mouth toward earth. Aiming it squarely at the demon, he called, “Great King Silver Horn!” The monster dared not refuse to answer and had no choice but to respond. In an instant he was drawn inside, and Pilgrim sealed the gourd with a slip inscribed, “By command of the Supreme Lord Lao: obey this decree with all haste.” He rejoiced inwardly, thinking, “My boy, today you too shall have a taste of something new.”

p.src: He brought his cloud down, took the gourd in hand, and, intent only on rescuing his master, returned toward the entrance of Lotus Flower Cave. The mountain paths were full of hollows and uneven ground; moreover, he walked with bowlegs, swaying from side to side, so that the contents of the gourd sloshed and rustled without cease. Why, you may ask, did it make such a sound? The truth was that the Great Sage Sun possessed a body tempered through long refinement, so he could not readily be dissolved; but though the monster could soar upon clouds and ride the mist, those were merely magical arts. In essence he had not yet cast off his mortal body, and once inside the treasure he dissolved. Pilgrim did not yet realize that the monster had already dissolved, and laughed, “My boy, are you pissing in there, or gargling? Old Sun has been through this business before. Until seven or eight days have passed and you have dissolved into thin juice, I shall not open the lid to look. What is the hurry? What is so pressing? Considering how easily I got out, I really ought not look for a thousand years.” Holding the gourd and talking as he went, he presently reached the cave entrance without noticing. He shook the gourd, making it rattle all the more. He said, “This sounds like a diviner’s筒 being shaken for a reading; it would serve nicely for divination. Let Old Sun cast a reading and see when Master will finally be able to leave this place.” See how he kept shaking it with his hand while ceaselessly chanting, “King Wen of the Zhou and the Book of Changes, Sage Confucius, Mistress Peach Blossom, Master Guigu.”

p.src: A lesser demon inside the cave saw him and cried, “Great King, disaster! Pilgrim Sun has put our Second Great King into the gourd and is using him to tell fortunes!” When the old demon heard this, terror scattered his wits and soul; his bones went limp and his sinews numb, and he fell flat upon the ground. Wailing loudly, he cried, “My dear brother! You and I secretly left the upper realm and entrusted ourselves to this mortal world, hoping to share glory and riches and remain forever the lords of our mountain cave. How could we have known that, because of this monk, you would lose your life and our brotherly bond would be severed?” All the demons throughout the cave wept bitterly together.

p.src: Zhu Bajie, hanging from a beam, heard the whole demon family weeping together and could not help calling out, “Demon, stop crying a moment and let Old Zhu explain it to you. The first to come was Sun the Pilgrim, the next was Pilgrim Sun, and the last was the Pilgrim called Sun. Those three words were merely reversed and rearranged; all three were my senior brother alone. He has seventy-two transformations. He slipped in here by changing his form, stole the treasures, and impersonated your younger brother. Your brother is already dead, so there is no need to make such a show of mourning. Hurry and scrub the pots and stove clean, prepare some fragrant mushrooms, other mushrooms, tea shoots, bamboo shoots, tofu, wheat gluten, wood ear, and vegetables, then invite my master and fellow disciples down. We shall recite a scroll of the Sutra of Rebirth for your brother.” When the old demon heard this, he flew into a rage. “They say Zhu Bajie is an honest fellow, but it turns out he is anything but honest! He is actually making sport of me and treating me as a joke.” He cried, “Little demons, cease your mourning for now. Cut Zhu Bajie down and steam him to a pulp. Once I have eaten my fill, I shall go and capture Sun the Pilgrim to avenge my brother.” Sha the Monk reproached Bajie, saying, “There now! I told you not to talk so much. The one who talks too much is to be steamed and eaten first.” The idiot now felt a good measure of fear himself. A little demon nearby said, “Great King, Zhu Bajie will not steam well.” “Amitabha!” said Bajie. Which good brother is accumulating such hidden merit? It is quite true that I will not steam well.” Another demon said, “Skin him first, and then he will steam nicely.” Bajie panicked and said, “I will steam well, I will! My hide and bones may be coarse, but once the water boils I will soon turn tender—soft and succulent!”

p.src: Amid this commotion, a little demon suddenly reported from outside the front gate, “The Pilgrim called Sun has come to our door hurling abuse again.” The old demon was startled again. “That rogue scorns me as though I had no one to defend me.” He ordered, “Little ones, hang Zhu Bajie back up as before, and see how many treasures we still have.” The little demon who served as steward said, “There are still three treasures in the cave.” “Which three?” asked the old demon. The steward replied, “The Seven-Star Sword, the Plantain Fan, and the Pure Vase remain.” The old demon said, “That vase is useless. It was meant to draw people inside when they answered its call, but we taught Sun the Pilgrim the spell, and he used it to draw my own brother in instead. We shall not use it. Leave it at home. Quickly bring me the sword and the fan.” The steward immediately presented the two treasures to the old demon. The old demon tucked the Plantain Fan into the collar behind his neck and took the Seven-Star Sword in his hand. He then mustered more than three hundred demons, great and small, ordering every one of them to shoulder spears, brandish staves, ready their weapons, and whirl their blades. The old demon himself donned helmet and armor and put on a blazing scarlet silk robe. The demon horde marched out in battle formation to capture the Great Sage Sun.

p.src: The old demon hastily ordered his underlings to deploy in battle formation and cursed, “You insolent monkey! You killed my brother and harmed my own flesh and blood. You are truly hateful!” The Pilgrim cursed back, “You death-seeking monster! You cannot bear to part with the life of a single demon. Yet my master, my two junior brothers, and even the horse—four living creatures in all—are hanging in your cave for no cause. How could my heart endure it? How could reason or feeling allow me to submit? Send them out and return them to me at once, add a generous sum for our travelling expenses, and cheerfully see Old Sun on his way. Then I may yet spare your wretched old demon’s life.” The monster would hear no argument and raised his precious sword to cleave the Pilgrim’s head; the Great Sage lifted his iron cudgel and met the blow. What a splendid battle they fought outside the cave gate! Ah!

p.src: The old demon and the Great Sage fought for twenty rounds without either gaining the upper hand. The demon pointed with the tip of his sword and shouted, “Little demons, attack together!” The more than three hundred fiends surged forward together and surrounded the Pilgrim at the center of the field. The splendid Great Sage showed no fear at all. Wielding his cudgel, he charged left and right, parried behind, and guarded before. The little demons all had some skill. The more they fought, the more closely they pressed him, clinging like wads of cotton to his body, seizing his waist and tugging at his legs, with not one willing to retreat. The Great Sage grew alarmed and at once used the magic of bodies beyond the body. He plucked a handful of hairs from beneath his left ribs, chewed them to pieces, spat them out, and shouted, “Change!” Every single hair changed into a Pilgrim. Just look at them! The tall ones wielded cudgels, the short ones swung their fists, and those too tiny to strike seized the demons by the shins and gnawed at their sinews. They scattered the little demons like falling stars and dispersing clouds, until all cried together, “Great King! All is lost; this is hard indeed, impossibly hard! The mountains and ground are covered everywhere with Sun the Pilgrim!” By this magic of external bodies, the demon horde was beaten back, leaving only the old demon trapped in the center. They chased him east and west until he could find no way out.

p.src: The demon panicked. Holding the precious sword aloft in his left hand, he reached behind his neck with his right and drew out the Plantain Fan. Facing southeast toward the Fire of bing and ding, directly aligned with the Palace of Li, he brought the fan down with a whoosh. At once flames blazed up from the very ground. So this treasure could summon fire out of nothing simply by being waved. The monster showed no mercy. He waved the fan seven or eight times in succession, scorching heaven and searing earth as fierce flames soared and surged. What a fire it was!

p.src: When the Great Sage saw this vicious fire, even he trembled with alarm. “This is bad! My true body can withstand it, but my hairs cannot. Once they fall into these flames, will they not burn as easily as singed fur?” He shook his body and drew all the hairs back onto himself. He left only one hair transformed into a false body to flee from the fire and draw off the danger. His true body recited the fire-warding spell, turned a somersault, and sprang aloft. Escaping from the great blaze, he sped straight toward Lotus Flower Cave, intending to rescue his master. He hurried to the entrance and lowered his cloud. Outside the cave gate he saw another hundred or so little demons, all with broken heads or fractured legs, their flesh split and their skin torn. They were all demons whom his body-division magic had wounded. Now they stood there groaning aloud and enduring their pain. At the sight, the Great Sage could not restrain his fierce and savage nature. He swung his iron cudgel and fought his way into the cave. Pitifully, the fruits of all their bitter cultivation toward human form were extinguished, and they became mere scraps of their former hides and fur once more.

p.src: After wiping out the little demons, the Great Sage burst into the cave to free his master. But then he saw flames blazing within and was so startled that his hands and feet fell into confusion. “It is over, it is over! The fire has spread in through the rear entrance. Old Sun will have no way to save Master now.” As he trembled in fear, he looked more closely. Ah! It was not firelight after all, but a beam of golden radiance. He composed himself and peered inside. It was the pure mutton-fat jade vase giving off light. Delighted, he thought, “What a splendid treasure! A little demon once held this vase on the mountain and made it shine. Old Sun obtained it then, but unexpectedly the monster searched me and took it back. So it was hidden here today, and it gives off light even now.” Just look at him! He stole the vase and, delighted with his prize, forgot for the moment to rescue his master. Instead, he hastily turned and headed out of the cave. He had only just passed through the gate when he saw the demon approaching from the south, precious sword in one hand and fan in the other. The Great Sage Sun had no time to dodge before the old demon raised his sword and struck straight at his head. The Great Sage hurriedly mounted his somersault cloud and sprang away, vanishing without a trace. Of his escape we shall say no more.

A little demon once held this vase on the mountain and made it shine. Old Sun obtained it then, but unexpectedly the monster searched me and took it back.
So it was hidden here today, and it gives off light even now.”
Just look at him! He stole the vase and, delighted with his prize, forgot for the moment to rescue his master. Instead, he hastily turned and headed out of the cave.
He had only just passed through the gate when he saw the demon approaching from the south, precious sword in one hand and fan in the other.
The Great Sage Sun had no time to dodge before the old demon raised his sword and struck straight at his head.
The Great Sage hurriedly mounted his somersault cloud and sprang away, vanishing without a trace. Of his escape we shall say no more.

In his anguish he raised his face to heaven and sighed; then, unable to restrain himself, he burst into loud lamentation: “What misery! What agony!” A poem bears witness to this. The poem says:

p.src: The old demon, overcome with shame and alarm, entered the cave weeping at every step. All the furnishings and utensils were still there, but the place was utterly silent, without a single figure in sight; its desolation made his grief more bitter still. Alone in the cave, he sat down and slumped over the stone table, leaving his precious sword leaning against its side and the fan tucked behind his shoulder. Sunk in gloom and silence, he fell asleep. Truly: A joyful event refreshes the spirit; when sorrow weighs on the heart, sleep comes often.

p.src: Meanwhile, the Great Sage Sun turned his somersault cloud about and halted before the mountain. Thinking of rescuing his master, he fastened the pure-jade vase securely at his waist and went straight to the cave entrance to investigate. He found both doors standing open, while all within was silent, with no sound or sign of movement. He immediately stepped lightly and slipped inside. There he saw the demon leaning against the stone table, snoring soundly in his sleep. The plantain-leaf fan had slipped from the garment at his shoulder and half covered the back of his head; the Seven-Star Sword still leaned against the side of the table. He crept softly forward, pulled out the fan, wheeled around, and with a whoosh dashed outside. But the fan’s handle brushed the monster’s hair and woke him at once. Raising his head, he saw that Sun the Pilgrim had stolen it, and hurriedly seized his sword to give chase. The Great Sage had already leapt out before the entrance. He tucked the fan at his waist, gripped his iron staff in both hands, and fought the demon. What a fine battle it was:

p.src: Only then did the Great Sage lower his cloud, charge into Lotus Cave, and release the Tang Monk, Bajie, and Friar Sand. Freed from their peril, the three thanked the Pilgrim and asked, “Where have the demons gone?” The Pilgrim replied, “The second demon is shut inside the gourd. By now, I expect he has already dissolved. The chief demon was defeated in battle just now and has fled southwest to Dragon-Subduing Mountain. As for the caveful of lesser goblins, Old Sun killed half of them with his body-multiplying magic; those few battered survivors who returned were also slain to the last by Old Sun. Only then could I enter this place and set you free.” The Tang Monk thanked him profusely, saying, “Disciple, it is all thanks to the hardships you have endured.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Hardships indeed. You merely hung there suffering pain, but Old Sun never once rested his feet. I have hurried back and forth, inside and out without cease, even more frantically than a courier at an express post station. Only by stealing their treasures was I able to rout the demons.” Zhu Bajie said, “Elder Brother, take out that gourd and let us have a look. Perhaps the second demon has already dissolved.” The Great Sage first removed the pure-jade vase, then took out the golden cord and the fan, and finally held the gourd in his hand, saying, “Do not look! Do not look! They once put Old Sun inside it. I pretended I needed to rinse my mouth and tricked them into lifting the stopper; only then was Old Sun able to escape. We must on no account open it, lest he too make a commotion and escape.” Master and disciples rejoiced together. They found the rice, flour, and vegetables stored in the cave, cleaned the pots and stove, and prepared a vegetarian meal. After eating their fill, they slept in the cave. Nothing more happened that night, and soon dawn came again.

p.src: Meanwhile, the old demon went straight to Dragon-Subduing Mountain and gathered all the she-monsters, great and small. He told them in detail how their mother had been slain, his brother imprisoned, the demon troops annihilated, and the treasures stolen by trickery. The she-monsters all wailed together. After grieving for a long while, he said, “For now, cease your lamenting. I still have this Seven-Star Sword with me. I intend to assemble all you female warriors, go behind Dragon-Subduing Mountain, and summon our maternal kin. We must capture Sun the Pilgrim and avenge ourselves.” Before he had finished speaking, a lesser goblin outside the gate reported, “Great King, your venerable uncle has arrived from behind the mountain at the head of a number of troops.” Hearing this, the old demon hurriedly changed into coarse white mourning clothes and went out in person to welcome him. This venerable uncle was his mother’s younger brother, known as King Hu Aqi. Patrolling goblins had reported to him that his elder sister had been killed by Sun the Pilgrim, who then assumed her likeness, stole his nephews’ treasures, and had been fighting them for days at Flat-Top Mountain. He therefore led more than two hundred goblin soldiers from his own cave to reinforce them, first stopping at his sister’s home to ask for news. No sooner had he entered than he saw the old demon dressed in mourning, and the two of them wept bitterly. After they had wept for a long time, the old demon bowed before him and recounted all that had happened. Aqi flew into a rage. He ordered the old demon to change out of his mourning clothes and take up his precious sword, then mustered every she-monster. Joining their forces, they mounted wind and cloud and headed straight northeast.

p.src: The Great Sage, meanwhile, had Friar Sand prepare the morning meal so that they might eat and resume their journey. Suddenly he heard the rush of wind. Going outside to look, he saw a band of demon soldiers approaching from the southwest. Greatly startled, the Pilgrim drew back and hurriedly called to Bajie, “Brother, the demons have brought reinforcements again!” Tripitaka turned pale with fright on hearing this and said, “Disciple, what are we to do?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Do not worry, do not worry. He told Friar Sand to guard their master and remain safely seated inside the cave, and ordered Bajie to take up his muckrake and go outside with him to meet the enemy.

p.src: The monsters drew up their battle formation, with King Aqi at their head. He had a fair, jade-like face and a long beard, brows like steel and ears like blades; on his head he wore a gold-linked helmet, over his body a coat of chain mail, and in his hand he held a square-bladed halberd. He cursed in a loud voice, “You reckless, impudent monkey! How dare you bully us so outrageously? You stole our treasures, harmed our kin, slaughtered our demon troops, and even dared to occupy our cave for so long. Hurry and bare your necks, every one of you, and accept death, so that I may avenge my sister’s family!” The Pilgrim cursed back, “You pack of furballs bent on dying! You know nothing of the powers of your Grandpa Sun. Do not run—take a blow from my staff!” The monster twisted aside to evade the blow, then met him head-on with his square-bladed halberd. The two advanced and retreated against each other on the mountaintop, but after only three or four rounds the monster’s strength began to fail. Defeated, he turned and fled. The Pilgrim pursued him, but the old demon intercepted him. They had fought another three rounds when Hu Aqi wheeled around and returned to the attack. Seeing this from the other side, Bajie hastily drew his nine-pronged muckrake and blocked him. Each took on one opponent, and after fighting for a long time without victory or defeat, the old demon gave a shout and all the demon soldiers closed in together.

p.src: Meanwhile, Tripitaka sat inside Lotus Cave. Hearing battle cries shake the earth, he called, “Friar Sand, go outside and see whether your elder brothers are winning or losing.” Friar Sand duly raised his demon-subduing staff, came out with a shout, and charged into the fray, driving back the horde of demons. Seeing that matters were going badly, Aqi turned and fled; but Bajie caught up with him and brought his rake down upon his back, making nine streams of fresh blood spurt forth. Alas, his true spirit departed for the road ahead. They quickly dragged him over and stripped off his clothes to look; he too proved to be a fox spirit.

p.src: When the elder demon saw that his uncle had been wounded, he abandoned Monkey, raised his precious sword, and struck at Bajie; Bajie blocked the blow with his rake. While they were locked in combat, Sandy charged forward and swung his staff at the demon. Unable to withstand them, the demon summoned wind and cloud and fled southward. Bajie and Sandy pursued him closely. Seeing this, the Great Sage hastily mounted his cloud and leapt into the air. Taking down the pure vase, he aimed it at the elder demon and called, “Great King Gold Horn!” The monster assumed it was one of his defeated underlings calling to him, so he turned his head and answered. With a whoosh he was drawn inside, and Monkey sealed it with a slip inscribed, “By decree of the Most High Lord Lao: obey with all haste!” The Seven-Star Sword fell into the dust and likewise became Monkey’s prize. Bajie came up to him and said, “Brother, you have the precious sword, but where is the fiend?” Monkey laughed. “It is all settled. He is already inside this little vase of mine.” Hearing this, Sandy and Bajie were overjoyed.

Please mount your horse, Master, and let us continue our journey.” Tripitaka could scarcely contain his joy. Master and disciples ate their morning meal, packed their luggage, readied the horse, and set out westward in search of the road.

p.src: As they traveled on, a blind man suddenly darted out from beside the road, came forward, seized Tripitaka’s horse, and said, “Monk, where are you going? Give me back my treasures.” Bajie cried in alarm, “We are done for! The old demon has come to reclaim his treasures.” Monkey looked closely and saw that it was none other than the Most High Lord Lao, Li. Startled, he hurried forward, saluted, and asked, “Where are you going, old sir?” The venerable patriarch at once ascended his jeweled Jade Bureau throne and hovered in the ninth heaven, calling, “Sun the Novice, return my treasures!” The Great Sage rose into the air and asked, “What treasures?” Lord Lao replied, “The gourd is for holding my elixir, the pure vase for holding my water, the precious sword for subduing demons, the fan for fanning my furnace fire, and the cord is a sash I use to bind my robe. As for those two monsters, one is the boy who tends my golden furnace, and the other the boy who tends my silver furnace. They stole my treasures and fled to the lower world. I had no means of finding them, but now you have captured them and earned yourself merit.” The Great Sage said, “You are truly an unreasonable old fellow. You let your own household loose to work evil; you ought to be charged with failing to keep them under proper restraint.” Lord Lao replied, “This has nothing to do with me. You must not blame the wrong person. The Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea asked to borrow them from me three times, then sent them here and had them assume the guise of demons to test whether you master and disciples were truly resolved to journey west.” When the Great Sage heard this, he thought to himself, “That Bodhisattva is thoroughly idle and troublesome. When she freed old Sun and ordered me to protect the Tang Monk on his westward quest for scriptures, I said the road would be perilous and hard to travel; she promised that whenever I faced dire trouble, she would come in person to save me. Yet now she has instead sent fiends to harass and harm us. She has not kept her word; no wonder she is doomed to remain husbandless all her life. Had you not come in person, old sir, I would never have returned them to her. But since that is your account of it, take them away.”
